reading.body:
AI litigation is argued out of precedents decided long before generative models existed, not out of new AI-specific law.

The two things this hub points to are a docket tracker and a set of older decisions. The tracker covers AI lawsuits in United States courts and refreshes daily from CourtListener. The precedents page names the cases defendants actually rely on: Sony for substantial non-infringing use, Campbell and Google Books for transformative purpose, Van Buren and hiQ for scraping, Zeran for Section 230.

The pattern is that the legal questions AI raises are being routed into existing doctrine rather than answered by new statutes. Copyright, scraping and defamation claims all resolve against tests written for VCRs, song parodies, search indexing and early internet speech. That matters for AI because the outcome of a case turns on how a model's training and output are characterized under those tests, not on the technology itself.

What this data does not cover is the substance of any case. It carries no parties, no rulings, no damages, no filing dates, and no count of active suits. The total field is zero and the points list is empty, so nothing here supports a claim about how much AI litigation exists or how it is trending. It also says nothing about compute, buildings or power. The connection to infrastructure is indirect at best: litigation risk shapes how training data is acquired and how models are deployed, but this data does not measure that.
